statement: Imagined movements of the left hand, right hand, both feet and the tongue produce distinguishable sensorimotor-rhythm changes and are the four motor-imagery classes used in EEG brain–computer interfaces (BCI Competition IV dataset 2a).
sources: Pfurtscheller G, Brunner C, Schlögl A, Lopes da Silva FH (2006). Mu rhythm (de)synchronization and EEG single-trial classification of different motor imagery tasks. NeuroImage 31(1):153–159 doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2005.12.003

statement: The hand area of primary motor cortex lies on the precentral “knob” about 4 cm lateral to the midline (approximate MNI coordinates ±37, −25, 58 mm, under electrodes C3 and C4), the foot area on the medial wall of the paracentral lobule next to the midline (under Cz), and the mouth/tongue area low on the lateral convexity (about ±55, −8, 36 mm); the drawing’s patch positions are these coordinates converted to the fsaverage head frame.
sources: Yousry TA, Schmid UD, Alkadhi H, Schmidt D, Peraud A, Buettner A, Winkler P (1997). Localization of the motor hand area to a knob on the precentral gyrus. A new landmark. Brain 120(1):141–157 doi:10.1093/brain/120.1.141

note_for_auditor: The MNI coordinates are approximate centres chosen by the site; check that each cited source supports the location statements attributed to it (hand knob on the precentral gyrus: Yousry; mouth region coordinates: Fox 2001; C3/C4 over the precentral/central region and Cz at the vertex: Homan 1987; foot on the medial surface: Penfield & Boldrey). Report whether the specific coordinates appear in Fox 2001 or Yousry 1997, and what those sources actually give.

statement: Before a self-paced finger movement the upper-alpha (mu) rhythm over the contralateral sensorimotor area begins to desynchronise about 1.75 ± 0.61 s before movement onset, beta power is attenuated in the 2.0 to 0.5 s before it, and after a brisk movement the beta rhythm recovers and shows a short-lasting synchronisation within 1 s. In cue-paced left/right hand motor imagery the cue-triggered motor-cortex activation starts about 300 ms after the cue and single-trial discrimination peaks about 1 s after it; the original Graz imagery BCI returned its classification within 1.5 s, and adaptive autoregressive classification carried a delay of around 1 s.

statement: A periodogram of N samples cannot resolve spectral details closer than 1/N cycles per sample (1/T in hertz for a record of duration T), and its variance is high and does not fall as the record lengthens; averaging the periodograms of L shorter segments (the Bartlett method; Welch’s method with windowed, overlapping segments) reduces the variance by a factor L and the resolution by the same factor, so the choice of window trades resolution against variance.
sources: Stoica P, Moses R (2005). Spectral Analysis of Signals. Prentice Hall Ch. 2 (periodogram resolution limit 1/N, p. 31; variance, p. 22; Bartlett and Welch methods, pp. 49–50)

statement: In the fastest flicker (SSVEP) spellers each selection takes 1 s, 0.5 s of stimulation plus 0.5 s for the gaze shift (60 characters/min, up to 5.32 bits/s), or 0.8 s with 0.3 s of stimulation (75 characters/min); the EEG epoch starts 0.14 s after the stimulus because of the visual pathway’s latency. The sensorimotor-rhythm BCI that reached three-dimensional control recomputed its spectrum every 50 ms from the previous 400 ms of EEG, and cue-paced motor-imagery competition data allotted 4 s of imagery per trial. Self-paced movement intention can be detected from the readiness potential about 500 ms before the movement.
sources: Chen X, Wang Y, Nakanishi M, Gao X, Jung T-P, Gao S (2015). High-speed spelling with a noninvasive brain–computer interface. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 112(44):E6058–E6067 doi:10.1073/pnas.1508080112

statement: The P300 is the largest positive peak within about 250 to 500 ms after a stimulus, about 300 ms after an infrequent target; in a row/column P300 speller with 100 ms flashes and 60 ms gaps, 15 repetitions of each row and column take 28.8 s per character, and the original Farwell–Donchin speller managed 2.3 characters per minute; averaging repetitions buys accuracy at the cost of speed.
sources: Polich J (2007). Updating P300: an integrative theory of P3a and P3b. Clinical Neurophysiology 118(10):2128–2148 doi:10.1016/j.clinph.2007.04.019

statement: The early readiness potential (Bereitschaftspotential) begins about 2 s before a self-initiated movement and its steeper late phase about 400 ms before; in Libet’s experiment the onset of the readiness potential preceded the reported moment of conscious intention by about 350 ms for fully spontaneous acts (about 800 ms with some preplanning), and that reported moment lies only about 200 ms before the movement.
sources: Shibasaki H, Hallett M (2006). What is the Bereitschaftspotential?. Clinical Neurophysiology 117(11):2341–2356 doi:10.1016/j.clinph.2006.04.025
